title: Database reviews start with scattered evidence

text: Database reviews start with scattered evidence
Schema structure, design concerns, and change history often live in different tools.
Teams need to answer four basic questions before they can make a safe design decision.
A comparison with the last scan
A readable explanation tied to evidence
Understanding a database takes more than seeing its tables.

Problem framing draws from PROJECT_PRIMER.md and the hackathon review guide in chat “Explain project for hackathon review.” The project targets schema understanding and review, not automatic database administration.

title: One saved snapshot anchors the review

text: One saved snapshot anchors the review
The workbench turns metadata into a record people can inspect, discuss, and compare.
Test access to an authorized database
Save schema metadata as a snapshot
Run repeatable checks on that snapshot
Explore findings, docs, diagram, and chat
Record decisions and compare future scans
Business tables and collections being inspected.
Connections, snapshots, findings, reports, conversations, and run history.

title: The shop demo makes findings concrete

text: The shop demo makes findings concrete
Four tables show ordinary relationships and one deliberate review question.
No declared primary key and a timestamp without time zone invite review. They do not prove the table is wrong.
order_items keeps product name and price from the purchase date. That history may be intentional, even if a catalog stores current values too.

Demo schema details and interpretation come from PROJECT_PRIMER.md and the supplied demo SQL under demo/postgres and demo/supabase_shop_schema.sql. The documented demo has two customers, two orders, and one order item. The relationship diagram shows table-level structure, not row counts.

title: Three kinds of reasoning share the work

text: Three kinds of reasoning share the work
Repeatable checks establish facts; human context and optional AI help interpret them.
Example: a table has no declared primary key. The output is a finding with evidence, assumptions, and a certainty label.
Normalization checks use confirmed functional dependencies. The result depends on whether those rules are complete and true.
With explicit opt-in, the model can inspect objects, findings, or business rules, then cite saved evidence.
The model has no general SQL execution or schema-change tool.

Reasoning model and boundaries come from PROJECT_PRIMER.md, backend/app/agent.py, and the project review chat. AI mode was not enabled in the recorded local run, so this slide describes the implemented design and its intended boundaries rather than a live AI demonstration.

title: The Design Lab helps investigate tradeoffs

text: The Design Lab helps investigate tradeoffs
Each report has a different evidence base, so its limits travel with the result.
Samples up to 1,000 rows per table
Sample may not represent all rows
Candidate needs plan and write-cost review
Not a benchmark or migration decision
Measures synthetic rows in SQLite or sandbox

title: Human review and database permissions set the boundary

text: Human review and database permissions set the boundary
The workbench records and explains recommendations. The target database remains under the operator’s control.
Use an authorized connection and read-only credentials for ordinary scans.
Limit returned rows, response size, and execution time; reject non-SELECT and locking queries.
Approvals and migration inventories record review. They do not apply schema changes.
A model key and explicit schema-sharing opt-in are required for external AI context.
A saved snapshot describes one scan. Rescan before relying on changed database structure.
Optional local accounts are not security-reviewed for public exposure; jobs run in one API process.
A recommendation can be useful and still require workload evidence or business context.

Boundaries and limitations are documented in README.md, PROJECT_PRIMER.md, and IMPLEMENTATION_STATUS.md. SQL parsing does not replace database permissions. The optional local account system lacks a security review, rate limits, external identity, backup/restore, and distributed workers.

title: Next: validate advice before broader use

text: Next: validate advice before broader use
The strongest continuation is broader live evidence and measured value for review decisions.
Exercise connector fixtures, schedules, auth, sandbox, and advanced design flows on disposable data.
Compare advisory finding triage and evidence-gap labels with human review on representative cases.
Improve authentication, secrets, persistence, worker coordination, and operational checks before shared deployment.
A database workbench that turns schema metadata into reviewable findings and evidence-linked explanations, while keeping changes under human control.
Jev decision support is being explored in a separate branch. Its live TypeSafe responses still need validation before presenting it as part of this build.
